taxonomy.subtopic: Left superior-division middle cerebral artery infarction with Broca aphasia

questions.stem_html: A 67-year-old right-handed man develops abrupt right facial weakness, right arm weakness, and nonfluent speech. He follows multistep commands and appears frustrated by his inability to speak. The accompanying vascular-territory map highlights the lateral frontal cortex anterior to the precentral gyrus. Occlusion of which vessel best explains this pattern?

options.text_html: Left anterior cerebral artery
Left posterior cerebral artery
Left middle cerebral artery inferior division
Left middle cerebral artery superior division
Left lenticulostriate arteries

questions.explanation_html: The superior division of the dominant middle cerebral artery supplies the lateral frontal lobe, including Broca area and adjacent face-arm motor cortex. Infarction produces nonfluent expressive aphasia with preserved comprehension plus contralateral face and arm weakness. Inferior-division MCA infarction more often produces fluent aphasia with impaired comprehension.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Anterior cerebral artery infarction predominantly affects the contralateral leg and medial frontal functions.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Posterior cerebral artery infarction typically causes visual-field deficits and may affect memory or the thalamus.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Lenticulostriate infarction causes a lacunar motor syndrome without a cortical aphasia.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Inferior-division dominant MCA infarction classically impairs comprehension and produces fluent, nonsensical speech.

questions.educational_objective: Dominant superior-division MCA infarction injures Broca area and lateral face-arm motor cortex, causing nonfluent aphasia with contralateral face and arm weakness.

taxonomy.subtopic: Subepithelial immune deposits with spike-and-dome basement-membrane remodeling

questions.stem_html: A 46-year-old man has progressive edema and 7.2 g of urinary protein per day. Serum anti-PLA2R antibodies are present. The accompanying renal-biopsy schematic shows granular capillary-loop immunofluorescence and basement-membrane projections between electron-dense deposits. Where are the deposits primarily located?

options.text_html: Within the mesangial matrix
Between the endothelium and glomerular basement membrane
Within the dense layer of the glomerular basement membrane
Along the basement membrane in a continuous linear pattern
Between the glomerular basement membrane and podocyte foot processes

questions.explanation_html: Membranous nephropathy is characterized by subepithelial immune deposits on the podocyte side of the glomerular basement membrane. New basement-membrane material forms between deposits, producing silver-stain spikes and a spike-and-dome appearance. Immunofluorescence is granular rather than linear.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Mesangial immune deposits are characteristic of disorders such as IgA nephropathy.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Subendothelial deposits are readily accessible to circulating inflammatory cells and are typical of proliferative nephritic lesions.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Intramembranous dense deposits suggest dense-deposit disease rather than membranous nephropathy.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Continuous linear IgG along the basement membrane is typical of anti-GBM disease.

questions.educational_objective: Membranous nephropathy produces subepithelial immune deposits and intervening basement-membrane spikes, causing nephrotic proteinuria with granular capillary-loop staining.

media.alt_text: Original light-microscopy, immunofluorescence, and electron-microscopy schematic showing membranous nephropathy spike-and-dome changes.

taxonomy.subtopic: Immune-complex complement activation with subepithelial humps

questions.stem_html: A 9-year-old boy develops periorbital edema and cola-colored urine 2 weeks after impetigo. Serum C3 is low. The accompanying biopsy schematic shows granular C3 and IgG staining in a starry-sky pattern and large subepithelial electron-dense humps. Which mechanism best explains the renal injury?

options.text_html: Deposition of streptococcal antigen-antibody complexes with complement activation
Autoantibodies binding uniformly to the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen
Mesangial deposition of galactose-deficient IgA-containing complexes
ANCA-mediated neutrophil activation without substantial immune deposits
T-cell cytokine injury causing isolated podocyte foot-process effacement

questions.explanation_html: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is an immune-complex disease. Circulating and in-situ complexes containing nephritogenic streptococcal antigens activate complement, producing low serum C3, granular glomerular staining, endocapillary inflammation, and subepithelial humps.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: Anti-GBM disease shows linear immunoglobulin staining and often pulmonary hemorrhage.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: IgA nephropathy usually follows mucosal infection by days rather than weeks and has dominant mesangial IgA.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis has little or no immune staining.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Minimal change disease causes nephrotic syndrome and diffuse foot-process effacement without granular immune deposits.

questions.educational_objective: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis results from immune-complex deposition and complement activation, producing low C3, granular staining, and subepithelial humps.

media.alt_text: Original schematic showing starry-sky granular immunofluorescence and subepithelial humps in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.

taxonomy.subtopic: Elevated intrapleural pressure causing mediastinal shift and reduced venous return

questions.stem_html: A mechanically ventilated patient suddenly develops hypotension, tachycardia, distended neck veins, and absent breath sounds over the right chest. The accompanying diagram shows right-lung collapse with leftward mediastinal displacement. Which change most directly causes the hypotension?

options.text_html: Reflex pulmonary vasodilation that reduces left ventricular afterload
Compression of the venae cavae that reduces right ventricular preload
Acute aortic compression that increases systemic vascular resistance
Loss of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction causing isolated arterial hypoxemia
Increased left ventricular compliance caused by reduced pericardial pressure

questions.explanation_html: In tension pneumothorax, one-way air entry raises intrapleural pressure, collapses the ipsilateral lung, and shifts the mediastinum. Compression of the venae cavae impairs venous return, lowers right ventricular preload, and causes obstructive shock. Treatment must not wait for confirmatory imaging in an unstable patient.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Pulmonary vasodilation is not the primary hemodynamic event and would not explain distended neck veins.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: The major vascular compression affects venous return rather than the aorta.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Hypoxemia occurs, but the profound hypotension is driven by reduced preload and cardiac output.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Tension physiology raises intrathoracic pressure and restricts filling; it does not increase ventricular compliance.

questions.educational_objective: Tension pneumothorax causes obstructive shock by increasing intrathoracic pressure and compressing systemic veins, thereby reducing venous return and cardiac output.
